item.title: 30+ Resources That Have Made Me a Better Marketer
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
Every time I chat with a fellow marketer, whether they're just starting out or have been in the game for years, they ask: "What are you learning right now?"

Honestly? It's always hard to answer because I'm constantly learning something. My brain is basically a content sponge with commitment issues.

But I decided to compile a list of resources that have genuinely made me a better marketer and communicator over the past year. This ranges from the popular names everyone's talking about to more niche finds that deserve way more attention.

Fair warning: narrowing this down was painful as I had to cut so many favorites. But these are the ones I keep returning to, the ones that have actually shifted how I think about marketing, storytelling and strategy.

Hopefully, you get inspired by this list. Or not. Either way, here we go.

People Worth Following (and Why)

Chima Mmeje

I've been following Chima since she made the bold move to leave the content mill where she was earning peanuts, and watching her evolve into a formidable force in the global content marketing space has been nothing short of inspiring.

On top of that, she makes you feel like you're sitting across from her at a coffee shop while she breaks down marketing frameworks. Her LinkedIn posts, for instance, read less like 'thought leadership' and more like letters from a friend who happens to be brilliant at all things content marketing.

Toluwanimi Onakoya

Now, Toluwanimi—or Nimi, as I fondly call her—is an outlier on this list because her content is more communications-focused than marketing-focused. But she's someone whose work I always look forward to because her approach is delightful. She has this cute, "everything-is-going-to-be-alright," feel-good storytelling style that makes her videos easy to digest, insightful and worth bookmarking.

Amanda Natividad

I recently read Amanda's new piece on framing and it reminded me exactly why I fell in love with her content in the first place. She has this gift for using storytelling and relatable examples to make complex marketing concepts feel obvious. If you're not reading her work, you're missing out on some of the clearest thinking in B2B marketing right now.

Rand Fishkin

The other day, I was reading SparkToro's latest research on tracking AI visibility, and it was so good it inspired me to refine a study I was working on. That's the Rand effect. Whether it's video or written content, his work makes data feel human and insights feel urgent.

James Praise

James breaks down frameworks, messaging hierarchies, and go-to-market strategies (via his newsletter, Marketing In Action) in a way that feels accessible without being dumbed down. That balance alone easily earns him a spot among my top favorite marketers, and his newsletter is one of the few I read immediately instead of letting it sit in my inbox for three weeks.


Ayomide Joseph

Ayomide writes about buyer enablement, which sounds boring until you read his stuff. He backs everything with examples and actual metrics. He's one of the few writers where I see their name and immediately stop what I'm doing to read, which is rare in an era where everyone's churning out content but few people are saying anything worth remembering.

Caityln Richardson

This is another outlier on the list because she's not a marketer or even a comms specialist, and she doesn't write marketing-related content. But I love her work because reading her feels like watching someone think through problems with exceptional clarity, and that's a skill that translates to everything, including how I approach crafting messaging and structuring arguments in my own writing.

Tami Oladipo

Tami and I first chatted when I interviewed her for an anonymous feature where she documented her income growth. She had just landed her role at Buffer and achieved an income that placed her as a top 1% earner in Nigeria, and she shared her experience so humbly and without holding back. Since then, I've been following her content, and that same expressive, no-BS nature shapes her current approach. If you want tips on the creator economy or need inspiration for how to position yourself authentically while building leverage, Tami should be your go-to. She's proof that you can be transparent about ambition without being obnoxious about it.

Luk Symers

Luk's content is good ol' writing—you know, the kind that existed before AI slop became a thing. More importantly, his work is filled with gems I've applied to my consulting services and even my personal life. His post "Why Relying On Your Network Is A High-Risk Consulting Growth Strategy" hit me like a truck because it articulated something I'd been feeling but couldn't name. His insights on authority-building, positioning, and sustainable consulting practices are some of the most pragmatic I've encountered, and they've directly influenced how I think about building my own professional leverage.

Ryan Law

From his days at Animalz, Ryan has always been one of those marketers I look up to and admire. Though his writing has evolved since then—he's moved from ideating conceptual frameworks to crafting detailed case studies and newsjacking trending topics—the quality has remained consistently high. His posts challenge assumptions, which is exactly what good marketing content should do.

Tim Soulo

Similar to Amanda and Rand, I can't help but include Tim on this list. He's been consistently excellent, but what I appreciate most are the podcast episodes he leads on the Ahrefs podcast. As someone obsessed with great conversations, Tim's interviewing style has earned him major points in my book. He knows how to pull insight out of guests without making it feel forced or overly scripted.

Peace Itimi

Peace has moved from marketing into founding her own thing (rivaaaa), but she remains a force in the African tech ecosystem. Her content—whether she's on a podcast, doing video, or writing—is a big reason why. Her ability to make marketing feel strategic yet human is something I aspire to in my own work.

Olabinjo Adeniran

This list won't be complete without Olabinjo, whose work I've closely followed since 2023. I first came across him on Twitter, then went down a rabbit hole and found his thoughts fascinating, especially his case studies. The deep dive on Flo's growth remains an all-time favorite.

Newsletters I Actually Read

Field Notes

This newsletter is an absolute favorite. The Omniscient Digital team uses vivid examples, metaphors, and analogies to drive their points across in ways that make every issue feel like a mini masterclass in content marketing. I've stolen more frameworks from Field Notes than I'd like to admit.

SEOFOMO Newsletter

With AI, zero-click searches, and Google's algorithm updates happening at breakneck speed, SEOFOMO keeps me in the loop without overwhelming me. Essential if you work in SEO or content and don't want to spend three hours a day reading industry news.

Demand Curve's Growth Newsletter

This newsletter breaks down growth strategies with actual examples and frameworks you can use immediately, which means it's one of those newsletters where I highlight half the email because everything feels relevant to whatever I'm working on that week.

Growth Memo by Kevin Indig

Kevin's newsletter sits at the intersection of SEO, growth, and product thinking. His deep dives are legitimately research-level quality (think 3,000+ word explorations of topics with original data and case studies).

Farnam Street (Brain Food)

Shane Parrish's newsletter is technically not a marketing resource, but it's made me a significantly better thinker, which has made me a better marketer. Every Sunday, I get mental models, decision-making frameworks, and insights from philosophy, psychology, and business all wrapped up in one beautiful email.

Podcasts That Don’t Bore Me

Product Marketing Life

This podcast by Product Marketing Alliance (PMA) features conversations with product marketers about the messy, unglamorous parts of the job, including the politics, the misalignments, the launches that flopped. It's refreshing and relatable in ways that most marketing podcasts aren't.

This Is Product Marketing

Another solid PMM podcast that goes deep on strategy, messaging, and positioning without being too academic or too hand-wavy. The guests are consistently excellent, and the hosts know how to extract practical insights.

Merriam-Webster's Word Matters

Understanding language, etymology, and how words evolve makes you a better communicator, full stop. On top of that, it's just fun to learn why we say things the way we do. If you care about writing—and if you're reading this, you probably should—this podcast will make you better at it.

Morning Brew Daily

Quick, witty, and keeps me informed on business news without requiring me to read a dozen articles or wade through paywalled content. Perfect for staying conversant on what's happening in the broader business world.

Huberman Lab

Andrew Huberman's deep dives into neuroscience, behavior, and performance have completely changed how I think about focus, creativity, and decision-making. If you want to understand why people behave the way they do—which, spoiler alert, is pretty essential for marketing—this podcast is gold.

Books I Keep Going Back To

Good Strategy Bad Strategy by Richard Rumelt

This book ruined me in the best way. Now I can't look at a "strategy deck" without asking: "Okay, but what's the actual strategy here?" Rumelt's kernel framework (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action) has become my mental model for everything from campaign planning to life decisions.

Obviously Awesome by April Dunford

The definitive guide to positioning, and I'm not exaggerating. April makes a complex topic feel straightforward and actionable, walking you through exactly how to position a product in a way that makes people actually care. I've returned to this book more times than I can count, and every time I do, I find something new that applies to whatever I'm working on.

Building a StoryBrand by Donald Miller

Yes, it's popular. Yes, everyone recommends it. And yes, it's still worth reading. The framework is almost too simple, which is precisely why it works. I use the BrandScript template for everything from landing pages to pitch decks.

Influence by Robert Cialdini

A classic for understanding the psychology behind persuasion, and it's still as relevant today as it was when it was first published. Cialdini breaks down the six principles of influence with examples that make the concepts stick, and once you understand them, you start seeing them everywhere—in marketing, in sales, in everyday interactions.

Thinking in Systems by Donella Meadows

This book isn't about marketing at all, but it's fundamentally changed how I approach problems. Understanding feedback loops, leverage points, and system dynamics has made me better at diagnosing why campaigns fail and how to fix them sustainably.

The Art of Thinking Clearly by Rolf Dobelli

A catalog of cognitive biases and logical fallacies presented in short, digestible chapters. It's endlessly useful for understanding why people (including yourself) make irrational decisions, and once you're aware of these patterns, you start catching them in real time.

Notable Mentions (The Weird, Wonderful, Useful Stuff)

How to Stop Feeling Behind in AI

A grounding thread that helped me stop panicking about AI and start actually learning it in a way that felt manageable instead of overwhelming.

Kinnu App

This app has genuinely made me smarter about life and influenced how I approach marketing. It's like Duolingo but for learning concepts across philosophy, psychology, science, and history. Weirdly addictive.

The Complete Guide to Building Skills for Claude

If you're using AI tools for work (and you should be), this guide is gold. It's helped me create better prompts, build custom workflows, and generally get 10x more value out of Claude.

How to Fix Your Attention Span

My attention span was cooked. I'd open a doc to write and immediately check Slack. Start reading an article and tab over to Twitter. This video helped me understand why that was happening and gave me practical ways to rebuild my ability to focus. Deep work is a competitive advantage now, and this helped me get it back.

How to Build an Intellectual Life

This video completely reframed how I think about learning outside of work. I used to feel guilty for reading things that weren't "productive" or directly tied to marketing. This helped me see that building a rich intellectual life—reading widely, thinking deeply, making connections across disciplines—is the work. It makes everything else better.

Enchanting Marketing

This has been my favorite blog for the longest time, and it's still absolute gold even in 2026. Henneke writes about persuasive writing, copywriting, and communication with warmth, wit, and exceptional clarity. Her posts feel like having coffee with a brilliant friend who happens to be an exceptional writer, and her examples are so good they've influenced how I think about making abstract concepts concrete.


There you have it. These are the resources keeping me sharp, inspired, and occasionally up way too late because I fell down a rabbit hole and forgot time exists. If even one thing on this list makes you better at your job or just makes you think differently, then compiling it was worth the effort.

Now tell me: what are you learning right now? What's feeding your brain? I'm always looking for the next thing to obsess over.

item.title: How to Win Your First 90 Days as a Content Marketing Manager
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
Beyoncé doesn’t walk on stage and start singing. Weeks before any performance, she studies every move, rehearses every transition and makes sure the first ten seconds of the show set the tone for everything that follows.

That level of preparation is what makes her performances look effortless.

Your first 90 days as a content marketing manager work the same way. They shape how leadership sees you, how fast you earn trust, and whether your work ties back to real business impact. But most new hires rush straight into performance mode, pushing out content before they understand the story they’re meant to tell.

When I joined RemotePass, I took a different route. I spent my first month studying the product, refining our ICP, and building systems that made content run smoothly. That slow start became my advantage.

Within months, I was leading high-impact projects like the Certn-RemotePass partnership launch and earning public praise from the C-suite.

This guide is the same 30/60/90-day playbook I used to move from “new hire” to trusted strategist. It’s practical, tested and built for anyone who wants to prove the ROI of content marketing without burning out in the process.

Want a quick reference? You can download the 30/60/90 checklist as a one-page PDF to keep your first 90 days on track.

Month 1

At RemotePass, I spent the first month studying the product, talking to teams and cleaning up the mess I inherited. It wasn’t glamorous, but it built the foundation that made every later win possible.

Start by Actually Understanding the Business

Don’t rush to publish. Spend your first few weeks studying the company from the inside out.

In my case, I spent hours reading everything I could find—brand decks, OKRs, investor updates, product sheets, customer stories, even old blog posts. Each of these docs revealed something different. Investor updates told me what leadership cared about. Product sheets showed me how we sold. Customer stories showed me what people loved enough to talk about.

I also joined product demos and onboarding calls, which helped me hear how the team explained our product and how customers described their pain points. Eventually, I started spotting gaps in communication. If customers keep asking the same question, that’s a content problem waiting to be solved.

At the end of that first month, I wrote my own version of the company’s elevator pitch in plain English. If I couldn’t explain what we did in one paragraph, I knew I still didn’t understand it well enough.

Once I could explain the product clearly, I knew I was ready to write content that connects.

✅ Pro tip:

Ask three people from different teams to describe what the company does in one line. If their answers don’t sound remotely alike, that’s your first clue your messaging needs work.

Talk to Every Team You Can

In my first few weeks at RemotePass, I set up short intro calls with people across Growth, Sales, Product, Customer Success and even HR. This was because every team sees the customer from a different angle, and those perspectives are gold for a content marketer.

Sales told me where prospects were dropping off. Product team shared what users loved and what still confused them. Customer Success explained the recurring pain points that ate up their time. Growth showed me which channels actually worked. Those conversations helped me see the full picture — what messaging resonated, what content was missing and where I could make the biggest impact fast.

I kept notes from every chat in Notion and started spotting patterns. The same questions, the same gaps, the same opportunities. Before long, that doc became the starting point for my content roadmap.

✅ Pro tip:

End every intro chat with one question: If content could solve one recurring problem for your team, what would it be? You’ll leave each call with real priorities instead of vague ideas.

Audit What You Already Have Before Creating More

Before you write anything new, understand what already exists. A content audit sounds boring, but it’s how you find quick wins and avoid repeating work that didn’t move the needle.

When I joined RemotePass, I spent my second week reviewing every channel — blog, social, email, landing pages. I wanted to know what was working, what wasn’t, and what had been forgotten. I tracked which pieces drove signups, which ones people shared, and which ones got traffic but no conversions.

Numbers only tell part of the story, though. I also paid attention to tone and structure. Did our Tone of Voice (TOV) sound consistent? Did the content still reflect where the company was headed?

A lot of what ranked on Google didn’t even match how we talked about the product anymore. That disconnect became my first fix.

By the end of the audit, I knew exactly which topics deserved an update, which ones needed to be retired, and where the gaps were. That clarity saved me from guessing what to create next and gave me a solid starting point for my content roadmap.

✅ Pro tip:

Find your top five performing pieces and figure out why they worked. Was it timing, topic, or format? Once you know, repeat that pattern until it stops working.

Tighten Your ICP and Sharpen the Message

During my audit process, I realized the Ideal Customer Persona (ICP) on paper didn’t fully match the people actually buying. The docs said one thing, the CRM told another story. So I sat with the Sales team and reviewed closed-won deals, retention data and testimonials. We looked at which customers were easiest to close, which ones stuck around and which ones were the happiest. Those patterns became the base for updating our ICP.

This exercise changed how I wrote and positioned content. Instead of creating for “everyone hiring globally,” I started writing for specific people: HR leads who hated compliance work, founders who needed speed, finance heads who cared about cost efficiency. Once I got that clarity, everything clicked.

I also drafted our messaging pillars and tone notes that guided how we talked — clear, confident, and human. Later, those notes evolved into our company-wide style guide automated with a custom GPT.

✅ Pro tip

Ask your Sales team to list the top three customers they love selling to and why. Then compare that to your marketing personas. If they don’t line up, your ICP needs work.

Deliverables by the end of Month 1:

✅ Content Audit Report

✅ ICP + Messaging Brief

✅ Company-wide Style Guide

✅ Content Operations Doc (cadence, tools, ownership)

Month 2

By your second month, you should already know how the business runs and what content gaps exist.

Now it’s time to turn all that context into action by taking the steps below.

Use Data to Build a Strategy That Moves Revenue

By month two, you’ve learned enough to move from learning to building. Your goal now is simple: connect content to business impact.

Most content marketers slip here. They jump straight into creation without backing it up with data. I didn’t want to fall into that trap at RemotePass as I wanted our content to move revenue-related metrics

I began with a SERP and competitor audit to see what our audience was actually searching for and what others were missing. I looked for keywords with intent but low competition, and topics our ICP cared about but that no one had owned yet.

Those findings shaped everything that came next.

From there, I built a content gap list mapping high-potential topics, their search intent and how they tied back to the RemotePass product. For example, when I noticed HR ICPs were searching for help with choosing a global payroll solution, I added a few simple explainers about it to our roadmap. Those posts became some of our strongest performers later.

With the data in hand, I built a quarterly roadmap aligned with company OKRs. Every piece had a clear purpose: lead generation, brand awareness, or activation. That focus made it easy to report impact and get leadership buy-in.

To track progress, I set up GA4 and HubSpot dashboards. The tools were already there, but no one was using them to tell a story. I changed that. Each month, I shared short reports showing how content influenced pipeline and engagement. Once stakeholders could see the numbers, they started believing in the work.

✅ Pro tip:

Build a “Content Impact” dashboard with three KPIs that tie directly to business goals such as qualified leads, assisted pipeline, and engagement by ICP. Keep it simple and share it monthly. Once you do, people will stop seeing content as creative work and start seeing it as revenue work.

Pilot Content Experiments

Once you’ve nailed the strategy, the next step is to test it. Month two is where you start publishing, but every piece you release should teach you something.

At RemotePass, I focused on a few high-impact experiments instead of flooding channels with content. I published a thought leadership article on global payroll where I interviewed industry experts, including the CEO of Toggl. That piece drove and built credibility fast.

Next, I created a sales one-pager the team could use during demos. Then I worked on two case studies, Podeo and Logitech, showing how we helped real clients scale across borders. Those stories became sals and PR assets, proving what we’d been saying all along.

Each piece had a clear hypothesis behind it. The article tested authority. The one-pager tested clarity. The case studies tested social proof. After publishing, I watched performance closely to know which CTAs converted best, which visuals got clicks and which formats held attention. Those insights shaped what we did next.

Early experiments like these do more than bring quick wins. They teach you what the audience cares about, how internal teams use content and what actually drives business outcomes.

✅ Pro tip:

Create a few strong assets, track what happens, and use the data to refine your next move. The best content plans are built on small experiments that worked.

Review & Iterate

After you’ve shipped your first few pieces, slow down and review what happened. This part separates content managers from strategists.

At RemotePass, I made it a habit to share early results with leadership. For example, when the global payroll article went live, I showed how it led to demo signups from regions we hadn’t targeted before. That kind of context helped leadership see content as a growth driver and not a mere creative exercise.

I also took feedback seriously. I asked Sales how the new one-pagers performed in calls. I checked with Customer Success to see if case studies were being used. Those conversations helped me refine the roadmap and double down on what worked.

Some pieces needed rewrites, others needed better distribution. Instead of seeing that as failure, I saw it as calibration. Every iteration made our content sharper, faster, and more aligned with what the business needed.

✅ Pro tip:

Host a short “content review” session every month with Sales, Product, and Customer Success. Ask one question: Which piece of content helped you most this month? The answers will tell you exactly where to focus next.

Deliverables by the end of Month 2:

✅ 3 Strategic Content Pieces Published

✅ Quarterly Content Roadmap

✅ Performance Dashboard

✅ Collaboration Templates (briefs, feedback forms)

Month 3

By month three, you’ve built trust and delivered results. The next step is scaling what works.

At RemotePass, this was when I automated half my workflows, built templates for everything and made sure everyone from Sales to C-Suite could see the impact of our work at a glance.

Establish Repeatable Systems

By month three, you should be moving from doing the work to building systems that make the work run on its own. That’s how you scale without burning out.

After a few months at RemotePass, I noticed I was spending too much time recreating briefs, outlines and reporting templates. This practice wasn’t sustainable. So I started documenting every process that worked. I created templates for everything: content briefs, feedback forms, post-launch reviews and reporting sheets. Each one took a few hours to build but saved me weeks down the line.

Then I brought ChatGPT into the mix. I used it to automate repetitive tasks like drafting the first version of content briefs, summarizing competitor research and turning product briefs into marketing-ready plans.

Over time, this turned into a content engine. Writers and designers had clear starting points, and I had fewer bottlenecks to manage. Even reporting got easier because the templates handled most of the structure.

That shift freed up time for deeper, meaningful work such as messaging, storytelling and optimization.

✅ Pro tip:

Document every process the first time it works. Use AI to automate the boring parts, not the thinking parts. The faster you systemize, the easier it becomes to grow your output without losing quality.

Make What’s Working Work Even Harder

Once the system is running, the next step is to make it better. Optimization isn’t about doing more. It’s about getting more out of what already exists.

At RemotePass, I reviewed our content library by funnel stage (awareness, consideration and conversion). It helped me see where we were strong and where we were missing opportunities. Some blogs brought in a ton of traffic but didn’t move readers anywhere. Others like case studies quietly influenced deals but never got promoted.

So I started fixing the flow.

Awareness pieces got better internal links and clearer CTAs to push readers further down the funnel. Consideration assets got fresh data, updated screenshots, and stronger visuals. Conversion pieces like case studies got turned into smaller, shareable snippets for social and sales enablement.

I also repurposed top-performing articles into videos, carousels, and email sequences. One blog later became a short video that drove even more engagement. The goal was to stretch every strong idea until it gave us everything it could.

Each month, I tracked what worked and what didn’t. Then I adjusted. Over time, this rhythm of review, repurpose and refine made our library sharper, lighter and more effective.

✅ Pro tip:

Once a quarter, pull your top ten pieces by performance and ask, how else can we use this? Update it, repackage it, or distribute it again. The best-performing content is often the stuff you’ve already made.

Be Visible

By month three, your work should be speaking for itself. But that doesn’t mean you should stay quiet. If no one knows what content is doing, they’ll assume it’s doing nothing.

I started the habit of sharing good news at every chance I got. When a blog hit a milestone, when a campaign outperformed expectations, or when a case study helped close a deal, I shared it. Small wins compound when people see them often.

I also shared a monthly SEO report across the company so everyone could see how our work was performing. It kept the momentum alive and reminded people that content was moving real numbers.

Outside internal visibility, I also looked for ways to get the company and leadership in front of the right audiences. For example, I pitched Wesley, our previous Head of Sales, to platforms like HARO so he could share his take on industry topics. That single pitch got him quoted in a few publications and boosted both his and RemotePass’s credibility.

Those small visibility plays built long-term trust and showed leadership that marketing could create value beyond the blog.

✅ Pro tip:

Visibility compounds. Share wins, tag teammates, and spotlight leaders. The more people see impact tied to your work, the easier it becomes to get buy-in for the next big idea.

Set a Long-Term Strategy

Once things are stable, zoom out. Month three is when you stop thinking in weeks and start thinking in quarters.

I drafted a simple six-month roadmap with projected KPIs. I knew quarterly goals could shift and we’d probably adjust along the way but it gave the team direction. The roadmap outlined what we’d focus on, how success would be measured, and what resources we’d need to hit our targets.

I also started looking for new growth channels. At that point, we were doing well with blogs and SEO, but I wanted to diversify. I recommended building a newsletter, exploring community partnerships, and testing co-marketing with HR and fintech brands. Those small steps helped us expand reach without stretching the team too thin.

To keep everything grounded, I set up a quarterly content retro. It was a simple review session that compared what we planned against what actually happened. It helped us stay accountable and align with leadership’s OKRs, especially as priorities changed.

By the end of the third month, we had rhythm, visibility and a plan that could flex as the business evolved.

✅ Pro tip:

Plan in quarters, not chaos. A six-month roadmap gives you direction, but retros keep you honest. Review often, adapt fast, and make sure every idea ties back to a real business goal.

Deliverables by end of Month 3:

✅ 6-Month Content Strategy

✅ Documented SOPs

✅ Company-Wide Content Reporting Framework

✅ Thought Leadership Initiatives Launched

Final Thoughts

This 30/60/90-day plan was how I set myself up to win as a Content Marketing Manager at RemotePass. It helped me go from learning the ropes to leading launches, earning trust, and driving results that mattered.

If you’re stepping into a new role, don’t rush to prove yourself with quick outputs. Focus on understanding the business, building systems, and showing how content impacts revenue. Once people see that connection, you stop being the “blog person” and start being a growth partner.

If you’re growing a content team, this framework can be your starting point. And if you’d like help adapting it to your company’s goals, I’m just a message away.

item.title: How to Turn a B2B Product Launch Into Sales Conversations
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
When Arrows relaunched in August, a LinkedIn commenter thought its redesigned website belonged to another company.

The confusion made sense. Arrows, a B2B software company known for customer onboarding plans and digital sales rooms, had introduced a new brand and an AI sales platform that helps sales representatives plan deals, prepare follow-ups, and keep opportunities moving.

The launch explained the new product clearly. Its founder demonstrated how it worked, and interested buyers had a route to sales. Yet the strongest quantified customer results I found on Arrows' website came from its older product.

Across the 15+ launches I coordinated at RemotePass, I learned to watch for this missing middle: the evidence buyers still need after a launch catches their attention. Relaunches make the gap wider because previous results cannot establish what a new product delivers.

I audited Arrows' relaunch from August 25 to September 24, 2026, scoring the public buyer journey from 0 (clear gap) to 2 (strong evidence). The analysis follows three questions buyers ask before moving toward a purchase.

1. Is this product actually for me?

Arrows' relaunch introduced an agent-native sales execution platform that maintains a gameplan for each deal and prepares the work needed to move opportunities forward.

The new positioning was direct:

Every deal gets a gameplan. Arrows gets it done.

In the version of CEO Daniel Zarick's launch post I reviewed on November 2, the announcement had attracted 220 reactions, 87 comments, and 20 reposts.

The product demonstration showed Arrows preparing follow-up work after a sales representative had forgotten to discuss pricing with a CEO. Another scenario involved assembling evaluation material after a prospect mentioned speaking to a competitor.

The following day, COO Kim Hacker expanded on the positioning, describing situations in which sales representatives leave meetings knowing what needs to happen next but struggle to maintain that context across multiple deals.

Her examples involved pricing objections, security reviews, and bringing additional stakeholders into evaluations. They gave prospective buyers a clear understanding of the work Arrows intended to handle.

I have analyzed founder-led LinkedIn performance across 530 fintech posts before, but here the comments offered more insight into buyer concerns than the engagement figures.

One reader asked what would happen to the original onboarding product. Another was the commenter who thought he had reached the wrong company.

Arrows had addressed product continuity in its launch announcement, explaining that existing onboarding plans and sales rooms would remain supported. Daniel also said customers had received an email about the changes in July.

The questions suggest that some of the audience still needed clarification, even with that information available.

Relevance score: 2/2. Arrows identified its target audience, explained a recognizable problem, and supported the positioning with examples of how the new platform would work.

The next challenge was giving those buyers enough evidence to decide whether the product would work for their teams.

2. Will it work for us, and can I convince the people who approve the purchase?

Arrows launched with a 1-minute-50-second product demonstration and reactions from pilot teams that had been testing the new platform on real deals. People familiar with the beta also appeared in the founder's LinkedIn comments.

Prospective buyers could therefore see how the product worked and find early confirmation that teams were already using it.

Then I looked at the customer results.

On Arrows' current customer stories page, Forecastr reports 20% faster sales cycles and a 10% increase in average deal value.

Those are useful commercial outcomes, but Arrows explicitly states that they came from its existing product.

The new platform makes a broader promise about automating sales execution. Results achieved with the earlier sales-room product cannot establish how effectively the agent-native platform performs CRM updates, prepares follow-ups, or maintains deal plans across a sales team.

Arrows labels the Forecastr results correctly, allowing buyers to understand which product generated them.

The disclosure also reveals a challenge companies face when repositioning. Their existing customer stories can support confidence in the business, but buyers still need evidence for the capabilities they are now being asked to purchase.

Arrows currently features a testimonial from Mitchell Kennedy at Filed, who reports that his close rate increased by 10% between Q2 and Q3 and credits the product with helping him identify overlooked deal work. That experience is more closely aligned with the new proposition, although I could not verify when the testimonial first became publicly available.

I also could not verify a quantified customer case supporting the new agent-native platform during its first 30 days.

For a sales leader evaluating whether to introduce Arrows across a team, that evidence would help establish what improvement the company could reasonably expect.

Buyers also needed to assess implementation and cost

In Kim's launch comments, one reader asked how Arrows could maintain reliable gameplans when the underlying CRM data was incomplete.

Kim explained that the platform could use additional context from conversations rather than relying entirely on structured CRM fields.

It was a useful response, although a team preparing for implementation would also need to understand how the platform handles outdated records, what changes require approval, and how its agents interact with existing systems.

Arrows' current pricing page explains that cost depends on the work being automated, the number of active deals covered, and the systems providing context. Buyers discuss those requirements with the company before receiving a price.

That approach accommodates differences in implementation scope. It also means a prospective champion needs a sales conversation to establish a likely cost, which can complicate early budget discussions.

An illustrative deployment and pricing scenario would make that conversation easier to prepare for.

On October 3, Kim published an account of running the company's sales process through Claude. She described an experiment involving two representatives who initially found Claude useful before encountering problems with repeated prompting, inconsistent context, different versions of shared sales skills, and the absence of a coordinated plan for each deal.

The article linked to an Arrows-versus-Claude comparison, giving prospective buyers a more detailed explanation of why a dedicated sales execution platform might be preferable to configuring a general-purpose AI assistant.

That article appeared 39 days after the relaunch. The comparison page was available by then, although I could not establish whether it existed during the initial 30-day window.

Later in October, Arrows also published material about promptless AI and the practical considerations involved in automating CRM updates.

Evaluation score: 1/2, provisional. Arrows provided product demonstrations and pilot feedback at launch. The first-month availability of quantified new-product evidence remains unverified.

For a company preparing a major repositioning, I would make a named pilot case study part of the launch requirements. It should establish the baseline, explain the implementation, and measure what changed after the new product was introduced.

That gives prospective buyers evidence they can take into discussions with the people responsible for approving the purchase.

3. What happens when I raise my hand?

Arrows provided a clear next step for people interested in the new platform. The launch included a demonstration CTA, while existing customers had a separate contact path for questions about their accounts.

Casey Drake, VP of Sales at Endear, commented on Daniel's launch post asking how to start testing the new product.

Daniel replied that Kim would message him.

That was a visible handoff from someone expressing interest to a named person who could continue the conversation.

Casey was also an existing customer, so the clearest public hand-raise I found was about expansion, not new pipeline.

In another exchange, a sales leader tagged several people who might find the product relevant. Daniel responded that Arrows was already communicating with two of them by email.

The team continued engaging prospects after the initial launch window.

On September 30, Daniel described an effort to revisit closed-lost opportunities. Using Claude, the team reviewed past deals and supporting CRM context to identify accounts that might now be a better fit for Arrows' new product. Kim confirmed in the comments that she had sent her re-engagement emails.

The relaunch gave Arrows a reason to email people who had already said no, about a product they had never been offered.

Arrows also refined its invitation to sales conversations. According to Visualping's pricing-page change history, an October 10 update changed the CTA from booking a product demo to booking an agent kickoff.

The newer wording framed the meeting around identifying the work Arrows would handle and planning the rollout. It gave prospective buyers a clearer sense of what they would accomplish during the conversation.

Visible-next-step score: 2/2. Arrows provided a clear public path toward sales and responded to expressions of interest. The score reflects that visible experience, rather than the effectiveness of its internal lead-routing system.

The Arrows scorecard

Step

Score

Finding

Relevance

2/2

Clear positioning and recognizable sales use cases

Evaluation assets

1/2*

Demonstrations and pilot feedback; quantified new-product proof during the first month remains unverified

Visible next step

2/2

Clear CTA, public handoffs, and later follow-up with previous opportunities

The evaluation score is provisional. Two other parts of a launch, whether sales can explain it and whether what buyers say reaches marketing, sit inside the company and cannot be scored from public evidence.

What I would add

For Arrows, I would prioritize three additions to the buyer's evaluation journey.

The first is a named pilot case study measuring outcomes from the new agent-native platform, with a clear baseline and implementation period.

The second is a dedicated comparison explaining how the new platform relates to Arrows' previous onboarding and sales-room products. The launch announcement already explained product continuity, but a standalone page would make the information easier to find.

The third is an example deployment with implementation requirements and indicative pricing. A sales leader should have enough context to begin discussing the investment internally before requesting a detailed proposal.

Who owns the first 30 days after launch?

Product marketing is often responsible for launch preparation, while sales carries the pipeline target. The two teams may share an interest in commercial outcomes, but their reporting cycles and immediate responsibilities differ.

Marketing can report campaign traffic and engagement within days. Qualified opportunities take longer to develop, particularly when buyers need internal approval or must compare several solutions.

The next launch may be underway by the time the first release has produced enough sales conversations to expose weaknesses in its messaging.

I would assign one person responsibility for the first 30 days after every commercially important launch.

That person would coordinate the work across Product Marketing, Sales, and Customer Success, with responsibility for identifying where buyers are losing momentum and making sure the relevant team addresses it.

Before launch: establish the handoff

Agree on what a qualified conversation should look like and which customer segments the launch is intended to attract.

The launch brief should explain what the product does and does not cover, while sales should be able to articulate the proposition to both users and decision-makers.

Define routing rules for different expressions of interest. Demo requests need an assigned owner and a short response window, while educational engagement can lead to further content. Existing customers may require a separate Customer Success route.

For a major repositioning, verify that the customer evidence supports the new capabilities being introduced.

Week 1: check who is actually entering the funnel

Review demo requests and the accounts entering sales conversations. Are they in the intended segment, and do they understand what the product does?

This is the check that would have caught our most persistent problem at RemotePass sooner. Some prospects booked calls expecting us to help them recruit, when our Employer of Record (EOR) service helped them employ and pay people they had already hired. Our marketing dashboards did not show it. Sales spent part of those calls explaining what we did not do.

If the wrong accounts are responding, fix the positioning and the channels bringing them in before spending more on distribution.

Weeks 2 and 3: examine what buyers are asking

Review call notes for recurring objections and questions existing content has not answered. Arrows' launch comments had already surfaced two: what happens to the old product, and how the agent copes with incomplete CRM data.

We eventually caught the EOR confusion this way. I worked with our Sales Operations Manager to build a reporting workflow connecting ChatGPT with HubSpot, and each week we used Collect → Validate → Act to pull recurring objections, category confusion, competitor mentions, and feature requests from call notes. Issues that appeared often enough to affect conversion went to whoever could fix them.

We created content and enablement material explaining what our EOR service covered, and repeated requests for time tracking gave Product more reason to prioritize a feature already on its roadmap.

Lead-to-SQL conversion improved by roughly 25% the following month, although a before-and-after comparison cannot isolate how much of that came from the messaging.

Week 4: examine what happened to interested accounts

Review the accounts that engaged with the launch and determine which progressed into qualified meetings or opportunities.

Look at where evaluations stalled and which evidence buyers requested that the team could not provide.

The review should produce a record of the problems found, the changes made, and any unresolved issues that need attention beyond the first month.

How to measure a SaaS product launch

Buyer question

Primary metric

Supporting signal

Is this for me?

Qualified conversation rate by target segment

Misqualified leads and category confusion

Will it work for us?

Evaluation-to-meeting conversion rate

Proof requests, objections, and evaluation-content engagement

What happens when I raise my hand?

Qualified meetings and opportunities from launch-engaged accounts

Response time and follow-up completion

These measures should use a defined cohort and attribution window, especially when the launch reaches accounts already familiar with the company.

Alongside them, check whether sales is explaining the launch the way the brief intended, and whether call-note findings are changing what marketing publishes.

By the end of the month, the launch owner should be able to explain which accounts responded, what prevented some from progressing, and what the company changed as a result.

The commenter who thought Arrows' website belonged to another company asked his question in public. Most buyers ask theirs in sales calls, which is why someone needs to be reading them.

Score your next launch before it goes live

Most of the gaps in this article are cheaper to close before launch day: who the launch is for, what proof buyers will need, where interest should go, and who will be reading the sales calls afterward.

item.title: Granola Growth Strategy: Can Product-Led Content Scale?
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
Granola gets an estimated 19.1K monthly organic visits from a remarkably small search footprint. About 88% of that traffic lands on the homepage, while the company ranks for 91 keywords and maintains a relatively small editorial estate.

Yet the product is growing quickly. In Ramp’s customer data, Granola ranks #2 for adoption in Sales Execution & Orchestration, with adoption up 21 percentage points year over year. It also ranks first for both new adopters and competitor switching.

That combination caught my attention. If Granola is gaining users without building the kind of large search and editorial machine common among competitors such as Otter and Fireflies, something else has to be creating the demand.

So I traced the system from its early VC wedge through onboarding, lifecycle emails, product launches, partnerships, search and AI discovery. The question became less whether Granola uses content and more interesting: what does content do when the product and its users create much of the pull?

Methodology

I audited Granola, Otter, Fireflies and Fathom in Ahrefs on 2 September 2026 using the same US database, comparing estimated organic traffic, top pages, homepage share and organic keywords. I then ran six buyer-style queries in Perplexity: four neutral category prompts and two Granola comparisons, recording inclusion, positioning and visible sources. These are directional point-in-time signals rather than market-share or causal measures. The Ramp figures cited earlier come from activity within Ramp’s own procurement and renewals dataset, so I use them as an adoption signal rather than a measure of the entire market.

The VC wedge made word of mouth intentional

Granola’s demand did not begin with a broad acquisition play. Its first users were venture capitalists, a deliberately narrow group chosen partly because of how much distribution each user could create.

Chris Pedregal has explained that VCs were attractive because they had frequent, fairly predictable meetings and were easy for the early team to reach. More importantly, those meetings connected Granola to founders, executives and other investors. One useful user could expose the product to several potential users through work they were doing anyway.

That distribution widened as the product grew. Founders adopted it, leadership teams followed, and by Series A, 57% of users were reportedly in leadership positions. Collaboration then gave the loop another route: shared meeting notes could land in Slack, where colleagues encountered Granola’s output before ever using the product themselves.

Granola’s current product keeps pushing in the same direction. “Invite teammates” and “Team up for free” turn an individual user into a potential distribution channel, while the pricing model increasingly rewards team adoption.

That helps explain the search data. Ahrefs estimates roughly 23,100 monthly organic visits to Granola, with about 20,600 going to the homepage. Someone searching for Granola may have first encountered it in a meeting, through a colleague, in a shared note or via someone they trust.

If much of the awareness is created before the search happens, then the blog is probably the wrong place to look for Granola’s content strategy.

So what is content doing?

Granola’s content becomes easier to understand when you follow what happens after someone encounters the product.

The first clue appears during signup. Granola asks users how they heard about it, offering options including friend or colleague, Reddit, LinkedIn, AI chat, podcasts, events, newsletters and articles. Those channels mirror the wider system around the product: recommendations, communities, founder-led media, events and editorial discovery.

Once someone gets in, Granola does not send them to a getting-started article. It creates a demo meeting with Sam Stephenson.

As Sam explains how Granola works, the product transcribes the conversation, asks the user to write deliberately rough notes and then improves those notes in front of them. The tutorial and the product demonstration are the same experience. By the time onboarding ends, the user has seen the core value rather than merely read about it.

Email takes over from there. The welcome message organizes Granola around the actual meeting workflow: what to do before a meeting, what happens during it and what becomes possible afterwards. Subsequent emails introduce Chat, folders, templates, follow-ups, meeting history and integrations as those capabilities become relevant.

Expansion gets its own content layer. Inside the product, prompts such as “Invite teammates” and “Team up for free” appear alongside the value of collaboration. The Business trial explains longer meeting history, stronger models and integrations at the point where an individual user can start bringing colleagues in. The copy is doing commercial work inside the product loop: moving the user from this helps me towards this could help my team.

Granola then turns what it ships into material for distribution. Its recent social activity is dominated by things people can use or experience: MCP integrations, templates, follow-up workflows, Delphi, the Apple Watch app and new product capabilities.


Granola also extends product distribution through partnerships, events and physical launches. Its Apple Watch strap, for example, gave existing users a tangible product moment to share, while firesides and community events put Granola in front of the same founder and operator networks that drive word of mouth. These reinforce a growth system that relies heavily on user advocacy and network effects.

That explains how content works inside Granola’s growth system. It still leaves a harder question: is Granola genuinely unusual, or is the whole category more brand-led than it looks?

Granola's search footprint is compact, but homepage concentration isn't unique

Granola’s search footprint is heavily concentrated around the product.

Ahrefs estimates 19.1K monthly organic visits, with 16,758 — 87.5% — going to the homepage. Pricing adds another 674 visits, while Explore and AI Note Taker contribute 389 and 378 respectively. The largest blog pages reach a few hundred visits each.

The competitor comparison changes how I interpret that concentration.

Otter is even more homepage-heavy: 91.3% of its estimated 186.4K organic traffic lands there, despite the domain ranking for roughly 2,100 keywords.

Fathom’s homepage accounts for 45.2%, but another 42.7% goes to /Overview, putting almost 88% of its traffic across two product-facing pages.

Fireflies takes a different route. Its homepage captures 67% of estimated traffic, with the rest spread across pricing, help content and hundreds of editorial pages covering meeting templates, integrations and adjacent workplace queries. It ranks for roughly 1,400 keywords across 344 pages.

Granola reaches almost the same estimated traffic — 19.1K versus Fireflies’ 20.5K — with 34 pages and 91 keywords.

There is a trade-off, though. Ahrefs records 141 AI responses for Granola, compared with 200 for Fathom, 996 for Fireflies and 1,800 for Otter. Those figures do not tell us whether Granola is recommended for the right queries, but they do show how much larger the competitors’ retrievable footprints are.

Search tells us Granola can capture substantial demand without matching its competitors page for page. It still leaves the harder question: what happens when the buyer does not know which brand to search for?

What happens when Granola’s name disappears from the query?

I tested that question in Perplexity on 2 September 2026 using four neutral buyer queries:

  • “best AI meeting notes app”

  • “What are the best AI meeting assistants for startups?”

  • “What are the best meeting intelligence tools for teams?”

  • “What are the best AI meeting tools for enterprise teams?”

I also ran “Granola vs Otter: which is better?” and “Granola vs Fireflies: which is better?” to see what evidence Perplexity used once Granola entered an active evaluation. This was a directional test of one answer engine, rather than a representative measure of AI-search visibility.

Granola performed strongest at the individual end of the buying journey. For “best AI meeting notes app,” Perplexity made it the strongest general recommendation, emphasizing its bot-free experience and combination of manual notes with automatic transcription.

That advantage became less pronounced when I asked “What are the best AI meeting assistants for startups?” Granola remained one of five prominent options, but Fathom, Fireflies, Otter and tl;dv appeared before it. Perplexity continued to associate Granola with bot-free, privacy-friendly meetings rather than broader team automation.

The positioning narrowed further with “What are the best meeting intelligence tools for teams?” Fireflies became Perplexity’s recommendation for broad team-wide intelligence. Granola was still included, but specifically for privacy-sensitive teams that dislike meeting bots, with a caution that it was less suited to a central enterprise conversation database or deep organisation-wide analytics.

The enterprise query makes the boundary clearest. For “What are the best AI meeting tools for enterprise teams?”, Microsoft, Zoom and Google led the answer, followed by standalone products including Otter and Fireflies. Granola appeared further down in a group with Fathom, tl;dv and Avoma as the evaluation criteria shifted towards SSO, retention controls, administration, data residency and governance.

The two direct comparisons expose another part of the content system. When I asked “Granola vs Otter: which is better?”, Perplexity had a clear understanding of Granola’s differentiation, but much of the evidence explaining that differentiation came from independent reviewers such as Zack Proser and Mrkt Correct.

The Fireflies comparison makes the contrast more pronounced. Third-party reviews again helped explain Granola, while Fireflies’ own comparison content appeared among Perplexity’s sources. In other words, Granola is earning recommendation without publishing a large comparison estate of its own, but competitors have more opportunities to participate directly in how the category explains them.

The issue, then, is not whether Granola can be discovered. It clearly can. The pressure point appears when the buyer moves from an individual who values a great note-taking experience to a team or enterprise buyer who needs evidence for governance, administration and organisation-wide use.

Where Granola could strengthen the model

Own more of the evaluation layer

Granola performs well when Perplexity is helping an individual choose a note-taking app, but third-party reviewers do a lot of the work when buyers compare it directly with Otter or Fireflies. Granola could publish stronger comparison, migration and use-case pages that give buyers—and answer engines—first-party evidence without turning its strategy into a high-volume SEO program.

Build content for the buyer Granola is growing into

The Perplexity test weakens as the query moves from individuals to teams and enterprise buyers. That creates a more specific content requirement: security documentation, administrative controls, deployment guidance, ROI evidence, customer proof and material designed for IT, security, finance and procurement. The individual champion can introduce Granola; these assets help that champion finish the sale.

Create more citable category evidence

Granola has plenty of product storytelling, but relatively little material that establishes how its approach compares with the category around it. Customer research, benchmarks, implementation evidence and technical explainers could give third parties and answer engines stronger material to cite without requiring Granola to become an editorial publisher at Fireflies’ scale.

What content teams should take from this

  • If most organic traffic lands on your homepage, stop treating the blog as your main acquisition engine. Granola gets roughly 88% of its estimated organic traffic through the homepage. In that situation, the first question is not “what should we publish next?” but “what is creating enough awareness for people to search for us by name?” Content investment should reinforce that source of demand.

  • If champions are bringing in the next user, build for the next person they need to convince. Granola’s product makes individual adoption easy, but the buying context changes as usage spreads across a company. The content required for a founder recommending Granola to a colleague is different from what security, finance or procurement will need before approving wider rollout.

  • If launches and product moments travel further than evergreen editorial, resource them accordingly. Granola repeatedly turns features, integrations, partnerships and physical activations into distribution. For teams seeing the same behaviour, product marketing, lifecycle content and launch creative may deserve more attention than maintaining a high-volume SEO calendar.

  • Test discovery without your brand name. Branded traffic can make visibility look healthier than it is. Run neutral category searches and AI prompts to see whether your company still enters the consideration set when the buyer has not supplied the name. Granola passed that test for individual use, but its position weakened as the query moved towards team and enterprise buying.

item.title: Does Founder-Led Content Work? Data From 530 LinkedIn Posts
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 State of B2B GTM Report surveyed 300 software and AI companies and found founder-led sales was the most common primary GTM motion, ahead of inbound and outbound. Among companies below $1 million ARR, 44% named it their primary motion; the figure was 26% for companies between $1 million and $10 million ARR.

LinkedIn is part of that shift. Half of respondents in the same report described posting by founders and employees as a core GTM channel.

That made me curious about one part of the playbook: what happens when founders and their companies publish on the same platform?

I analysed 530 LinkedIn posts from six FinTech companies and their founders between April and September 2026. Founder posts had higher median engagement at every company, with the premium ranging from 1.9x at Mercury to 11.2x at Ramp.

Once I compared posts against each account’s normal performance, the simple founder-content story started to break apart. Brand pages often got more lift from the same announcement. Personal perspective had a weaker relationship with performance than I expected. One finding I liked enough to start writing around disappeared when I inspected the posts inside the category.

I had confused important news with good product content.

The analysis also gave me a measurement method I think marketing teams can use: compare each post against that account’s six-month median rather than judging founder and brand on one scoreboard.

How I Analysed 530 Founder and Brand LinkedIn Posts

I studied Ramp, Mercury, Airwallex, Moniepoint, Increase, and Expensify alongside Eric Glyman, Immad Akhund, Jack Zhang, Tosin Eniolorunda, Darragh Buckley, and David Barrett.

I chose companies where both the founder and corporate account published enough during the six-month period to support comparison. The findings therefore describe active founder-led publishing programmes rather than B2B companies in general.

October posts were excluded, and duplicate captures of the same post were removed. The final dataset contains 166 founder posts and 364 company-page posts.

Engagement means visible reactions, comments, and reposts. I used medians because a few breakout posts can distort averages.

I also needed one way to compare a 2,000-engagement Tosin post with a 100-engagement Darragh post without pretending those accounts operate at the same scale.

So throughout the article, performance index means how a post performed against that account’s six-month median.

What is a founder content performance index? A founder content performance index compares a LinkedIn post’s engagement with that account’s six-month median. A score of 1.0x means the post performed at the account’s normal level; 2.0x means it generated twice the usual engagement.

A score of 1.0x means the post matched the account’s normal performance. A score of 2.0x means it generated twice the median engagement.

For matched announcements, I removed the post being evaluated before calculating the baseline.

I also coded the 166 founder posts for personal perspective using one rule: the founder had to contribute experience, judgment, interpretation, or a decision beyond reporting the news. I assigned those labels without using engagement performance to decide the category.

I remain the only coder, so I treat that part of the analysis as directional until someone independently recodes a sample.

The study also measures engagement volume rather than audience quality. LinkedIn gives me a comment count; it does not tell me whether those comments came from CFOs considering the product, employees cheering their boss, or founders networking with one another.

The median founder premium across the six companies was around 6x. I would use that as context rather than a benchmark. Six companies cannot tell a VP Marketing that their founder should outperform the brand by 6x, although the range gives teams something to compare with their accounts.

Follower count was the first explanation I checked.

Eric Glyman had around 45,000 followers when I collected the audience data, while Ramp had roughly 367,000. Jack Zhang had about 77,000 compared with Airwallex’s 199,000. David Barrett had roughly 16,000 compared with Expensify’s 23,000.

Five of the six founders had smaller audiences than their company pages, so larger founder followings could not account for the raw advantage.

A Refine Labs self-study found a similar pattern across seven employee accounts. The personal profiles averaged 2.75x more impressions and 5x more engagement than the company page despite having 46% fewer followers. It is a single-company analysis, so its ratios should stay inside that context, although the direction matches what I found here.

That one was interesting to see from Lagos. Tosin and Moniepoint had the closest founder-to-brand audience sizes in the sample, around 268,000 and 288,000 followers, yet his median engagement was still more than 10x the company page’s.

Moniepoint gives the dataset an African case where the founder advantage appears without a large follower imbalance, showing that the pattern also exists outside the US startup companies that dominate conversations about founder-led growth.

Matched Launches Changed What “Winning” Meant

I found nine cases where the founder and company account covered the same announcement.

Ramp Stack is where that stopped feeling like enough information.

Eric’s post generated 2,067 engagements compared with 702 for Ramp.

His performance index was 1.63x, while Ramp’s was 5.28x.

The founder delivered more people, while the company page had a post that travelled much further above its normal level.

I repeated that calculation across the matched set and found the company page had the higher performance index in six of nine cases.

That changed how I would report a founder program internally. If the CEO normally generates 2,000 engagements, a 1,200-engagement launch has underperformed their baseline even when the company version gets 150.

How to Calculate a Founder Content Performance Index

Ramp Stack gave me a method I would use in a marketing team.

You can calculate it without analytics software:

  1. Export six months of posts from the founder account and company page, then calculate total engagement for each post.

  2. Find the median engagement for each account.

  3. When evaluating a post, remove it from the baseline calculation.

  4. Divide the post’s engagement by the remaining median.

If the founder’s median is 1,000 engagements and a launch gets 1,600, the performance index is 1.6x.

Run the same calculation for the company page.

Keep raw engagement beside it. A founder post with a 0.8x index may still deliver far more attention than a brand post at 4.0x, while the brand team should still know they produced one of the page’s strongest posts.

The founder premiums in this sample ranged from 1.9x to 11.2x, with a median around 6x. I would not use 6x as a target because a smaller premium can also mean the company page performs well. Mercury is the obvious example.

The performance index travels better because each account competes with its history.

Mercury Checkbooks Was the One Near-Tie

Mercury’s checkbook launch was the only matched event where the brand came close to the founder. Immad generated 375 engagements and Mercury generated 348, a founder premium of just 1.08x.

The next closest pair, Mercury real-time payments, was already at 2.18x.

Both posts also outperformed their usual baselines. Immad’s performance index was 2.62x, while Mercury’s was 4.61x.

The product itself may explain part of that result. Mercury had spent years building a modern banking product, then announced physical business checkbooks.

Immad adds context. He talks about watching founder tools improve for years while checkbooks barely changed because people assumed they were disappearing.

The company page had a product announcement that was odd enough to get attention without borrowing much narrative from the founder.

Personal Perspective Helped, but the Effect Was Uneven

Of the 166 founder posts, 69 contained personal perspective and 97 did not.

Posts with personal perspective had a median performance index of 1.07x, compared with 0.82x for the rest.

The ranges overlap heavily, and the founder-level results split. Perspective performed better for four of the six founders. Jack Zhang and Tosin Eniolorunda saw the reverse.

Jack’s gap was substantial. His 13 perspective posts had a median performance index of 0.60x, compared with 1.18x for his other 30 posts. One of those posts came after the Semafor World Economy Summit, where he argued that “the world is rewiring” and that startups increasingly need financial infrastructure built for global operations from day one. It generated 198 engagements, around 0.50x his median.

Tosin gives a different version of the same problem. In one post, he wrote about spending his childhood taking things apart, rebuilding them, and carrying that curiosity into his work. It generated 600 engagements, around 0.27x his median.

These are credible founder posts. They contain experience, judgment and a point of view. Their performance still varied widely.

That is the part marketers should care about. “Add a personal story” is too weak a brief. A founder can share something personal or opinionated and still produce a post that does little relative to their normal performance.

The stronger test is whether the perspective gives the reader something they could not get from the company account.

That could be a decision the founder made, a pattern they have seen across customers, a market belief they are willing to defend, or context behind why the company is making a move.

A 2025 Edelman–LinkedIn study found that 86% of hidden decision-makers wanted thought leadership that challenged their assumptions, while 64% trusted thought leadership more than conventional marketing materials when assessing a vendor’s capabilities. LinkedIn helped produce the study, so I treat it as supporting context.

For a content team, I’d use one test:

What does the founder know, believe, or remember that changes how the reader understands the topic?

If the answer is weak, the personal detail is probably unnecessary.


My Product-Content Finding Fell Apart When I Dissected the Posts

My first category analysis showed company and product posts with a 1.29x performance index, ahead of the other founder-content categories.

I liked the result because it gave me a counterintuitive argument. Founders could talk about the business without becoming LinkedIn diarists, and I had a number to prove it.

I had started drafting that section when I went back into the spreadsheet to pull examples.

One of the “product” winners was a funding round. Another was a major launch. Then I hit an acquisition.

At that point the problem was hard to miss: I had grouped routine product updates with events that came with investors, employee amplification, press coverage, and a reason to care before the founder typed anything.

A convenient finding had been sitting on a bad category.

I split the posts again.

Major company events: 1.77x median performance index

Routine company/product posts: 0.99x

The original product-content advantage disappeared.

That changes the recommendation. A founder does not need to become the distribution layer for every feature update. Funding rounds, acquisitions, expansions, and major launches begin with more audience interest than routine product news.

This is also where the 2026 State of B2B GTM Report adds context. Founder-led selling is most common earlier in the company journey, when the founder’s relationships and reputation still carry more GTM weight. Content can extend that distribution when the company has something people care about.

How Founder and Brand Accounts Should Work Together on Launch Day

The matched events point to a simple launch-day principle: important announcements should usually use both channels, but the founder and company account should not publish versions of the same post.

The company account should handle the durable announcement. It can explain what launched, who it is for, what changed, and where the reader should go next.

The founder account should contribute material the company page cannot reproduce as credibly.

The test I keep coming back to is:

If I remove the founder’s name, what does the post lose?

If the answer is reach, that may be enough for a major launch. If the answer also includes context, the founder post has a stronger reason to exist.

Moniepoint can announce the ORDA acquisition, while Tosin can explain that he knew the founders years before the deal and had already seen the operating problem they were trying to solve.


That difference matters because the matched-event data already shows that founder and brand posts can succeed in different ways. Founders won raw engagement in all nine pairs, while brand posts produced the higher performance index in six. A launch plan should therefore give each channel a role rather than asking both to tell the same story.

The dataset cannot support a sequencing rule. Several source posts were preserved with relative ages such as “4mo” rather than exact timestamps, so I cannot tell whether founder-first, brand-first, or same-day publishing performed better.

Teams with access to timestamps can test that themselves. I would start by comparing three things across launches: publication order, time gap between posts, and performance index for each account.

The part I would avoid is drafting one announcement and then asking the founder to personalise it. That usually gives you duplicate distribution instead of a second useful angle.

Founder Content Belongs in the GTM System

The 2026 State of B2B GTM Report found founder-led sales was the most common primary GTM motion in its sample, while half of respondents already treated founder and employee posting as a core channel.

My dataset points in the same direction. Across 530 posts, founders had higher median engagement at all six FinTechs and led all nine matched announcements on raw engagement, usually with smaller audiences than the company page.

The advantage still needs context. Brand pages often saw more lift against their baselines, personal perspective was inconsistent, and routine product posts performed around normal levels. Mercury’s checkbook launch came within 27 engagements of matching the founder.

For a CMO or VP Marketing, the useful questions are:

  • Does this moment need the founder’s distribution?

  • What can the founder add that the company account cannot?

  • How did both accounts perform against their baselines?

Then connect the content data to the business. Public engagement shows attention. Your GTM team can see whether target accounts engaged, sales reused the post, or the content helped create demand.

I’m extending this research, so if you run the performance index on your accounts, send me the numbers. I may include them in the next study.

I also work with B2B companies on founder-led content, executive thought leadership, original research, and content strategy, including the measurement and content systems behind them.

Work with me

Send me your data
