item.title: AEO vs GEO: A Simple Guide to How AI Search Works
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
I first came across the term Generative Engine Optimization while working at RemotePass. Our search impressions were going up, our clicks were going in the opposite direction, and some of our content had started appearing inside Google’s AI Overviews.

I wanted to understand what the hell was happening, so I went down the GEO and AEO rabbit hole.

After RemotePass, I joined Xofu, an AI visibility platform by Citation Labs, where I led product marketing. That forced me to understand AI search beyond the surface-level advice you see floating around LinkedIn, and even after leaving, I kept digging into the discipline. I’ve since co-authored the first State of AI Search in Nigeria report and taught an AI Visibility Sprint at Treford, with a course coming soon.

I’m still learning because this field is moving ridiculously fast, but one thing I’ve noticed is how unnecessarily confusing people make it sound. Even marketers who understand SEO can hear terms like GEO, AEO, LLM visibility and retrieval and immediately feel like they’ve walked into a computer science lecture they didn’t sign up for.

So this is my attempt to explain the whole thing in a way my 15-year-old self would understand.

Let’s start with how people search

Imagine you want to know the best savings app.

A few years ago, you would probably open Google and type something like best savings apps. Google would return a list of websites, you would open a few of them, compare what they said and eventually make up your mind.

SEO grew around that behaviour. Companies created pages, Google organised and ranked them, and marketers competed for those rankings because appearing near the top usually meant more people visiting your website.

Now imagine asking ChatGPT:

What savings app would you recommend for someone who struggles to save consistently?

Instead of giving you ten websites to inspect yourself, it can compare the options, mention specific features and recommend something based on what you told it.

The website still has a role, but there is now another layer sitting between the search and the click.

Pew Research Center analysed almost 69,000 Google searches from 900 U.S. adults and found that users clicked a traditional result on 15% of visits without an AI summary, compared with 8% when one appeared. Links inside the AI summary itself were clicked on just 1% of visits.

Ahrefs found that the presence of an AI Overview correlated with a 58% lower average click-through rate for the top-ranking page in its analysis of 300,000 keywords.

I saw a version of this at RemotePass, where we became more visible in search while receiving fewer clicks, which meant rankings and traffic were no longer telling the entire story.

So what the hell are AEO and GEO?

AEO means Answer Engine Optimization.

The idea is simple: structure and communicate your information in a way that makes it easier for search and answer systems to use when somebody asks a question. Featured snippets, voice answers and some AI-generated responses all fall somewhere inside that world.

GEO means Generative Engine Optimization.

It focuses more specifically on increasing the chances that your brand, content or information appears inside responses generated by tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode or Perplexity.

Researchers from Princeton, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi helped popularise the term through the original GEO research paper. The original GEO researchers tested several ways of improving content visibility inside generative-engine responses and reported gains of up to 40%. The useful part is that the effectiveness varied by domain, which is another reason I wouldn't turn the findings into some stupid universal checklist.

Don’t become too attached to the terminology, though. Even the industry cannot agree on what to call the discipline. Depending on who you speak to, you’ll hear GEO, AEO, AI Search Optimization, LLM Optimization or simply SEO.

I find it easier to think about the job rather than the acronym.

SEO helps people find your page. AEO makes your information easier to use when answering a question, while GEO focuses on increasing the chances that your brand, information or point of view becomes part of an AI-generated response.

There is a huge amount of overlap between them.

How does an AI answer your question?

Imagine an extremely well-read student sitting an open-book exam.

The student knows a lot from everything they studied before the exam. When the lecturer asks something they need more information about, they can also open books, search for additional sources, compare what those sources say and then write an answer in their words.

AI search works in a similar way, although the technical process behind it is obviously much more complicated.

A model may know something about your company from its training data. Depending on the product and question, it may also search the web for newer or more specific information before generating the answer.

OpenAI describes ChatGPT Search as using web sources and search providers to find relevant information when responding to queries. Google has also explained that AI Mode can use something called query fan-out, where a complicated question gets broken into several smaller searches that are investigated before the system combines the findings.

Now, ask:

What is the best payroll platform for a 50-person startup hiring across Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and the UK?

An AI system may effectively investigate several things at once: international payroll software, Nigerian employment, Saudi compliance, UK payroll, product pricing, company reviews, available features and other relevant questions.

Think of GEO as building an evidence trail

Go back to our well-read student.

Imagine ten credible websites say that your company supports payroll in Saudi Arabia. Your own website explains exactly how it works, customers discuss their experience on review platforms, journalists have covered the company and you have published useful research about Saudi employment.

The student has plenty to work with.

Now imagine your entire website says things like:

Unlocking tomorrow’s workforce through transformative human-first innovation.

Fantastic. Nobody knows what the fuck you do.

If there is very little useful information elsewhere on the web, the AI has even less evidence to rely on.

A large part of GEO therefore comes down to making your company easy to understand and creating enough credible evidence around it that an AI system can confidently use your information when answering relevant questions.

That evidence can come from your website, but it can also come from research, news coverage, reviews, Reddit discussions, YouTube videos, comparison pages, documentation and other third-party sources.

I increasingly think about GEO as managing an evidence ecosystem around your brand.

Being mentioned, cited and recommended are different things

This is one of the most useful concepts to understand.

If somebody asks ChatGPT about savings apps in Nigeria and it says PiggyVest is one of the available options. PiggyVest has been mentioned.

If the answer links to a PiggyVest page while explaining one of its features, PiggyVest has been cited.

If the response says PiggyVest may be a good choice for someone who wants automated savings, it has been recommended.

Those three outcomes do not always happen together.

An AI system could recommend your company while using Reddit, G2 and TechCrunch as supporting evidence. It could also cite a research report from your company without recommending your product at all.

That is why measuring AI visibility purely by asking, “Does ChatGPT mention us?” leaves a lot unanswered.

I also want to know what the AI says about the company, what sources influence that description, whether competitors appear more frequently, whether the information is accurate and which brands are actually being recommended when buying questions come up.

Zach Chahalis from iPullRank summed up part of the shift well when he said:

“We’ve moved from, ‘Do we rank?’ to, ‘Are we cited?’”

I would extend that question further: are people seeing you, understanding you correctly and being given a reason to consider you?

Does this mean SEO is dead?

No.

Please don’t fire your SEO person because ChatGPT exists.

Google itself says the same SEO fundamentals used for normal Search continue to apply to its AI experiences. Pages generally still need to be crawlable, indexed and eligible for normal search results before they can appear as supporting links inside AI Overviews or AI Mode.

Google has even warned marketers to focus on effective SEO practices instead of chasing random “AEO/GEO hacks.”

The basics still do a lot of heavy lifting. Your website needs to work properly, search engines need to understand it, your content should answer real questions, your information should be accurate and your company should have some level of authority.

GEO simply stretches the job further into areas marketers may previously have treated separately, including digital PR, brand reputation, third-party mentions, original research, reviews and how clearly information about your company exists across the web.

What can marketers actually do?

The first tip is painfully simple: say what you do clearly.

If your software helps startups pay contractors across multiple countries, write that somewhere machines and humans can easily understand. You do not need to turn every product page into corporate poetry about “unlocking limitless possibilities across a borderless future.”

Clear information gives machines something useful to work with.

The second thing is creating material worth retrieving.

Original research, useful statistics, clear product information, expert commentary, comparisons, examples, definitions and firsthand experience all give an AI system more substance than another generic article repeating what the rest of the internet already said.

The original GEO researchers tested different ways of improving content visibility inside generative engines and found that approaches involving citations, quotations and statistics could improve visibility significantly in parts of their benchmark. The results varied depending on the type of query, which is important because it means there is no universal checklist you can mindlessly apply to every page.

Please do not read that study and start throwing random statistics into every paragraph.

The third thing is paying attention to what other people say about you.

Pew’s analysis of Google AI summaries found that platforms including Wikipedia, YouTube and Reddit appeared regularly among cited sources. Other research and industry experiments have repeatedly shown AI systems drawing heavily from reviews, forums, publications and other third-party websites when explaining or comparing brands.

Your website tells the internet what you claim about yourself.

The rest of the internet gives AI systems additional evidence about whether those claims make sense.

There is no secret button for ranking in ChatGPT

This is where the conversation gets less sexy.

Nobody outside these companies knows the complete recipe behind every ChatGPT recommendation, Gemini answer or Google AI Overview.

Models change. Retrieval systems change. Sources change. Prompts change. The same person can ask a question twice and receive slightly different answers.

Google has openly said that its AI experiences can use different models and techniques depending on the query. Research from tools such as Ahrefs has also shown considerable volatility in the sources appearing inside AI Overviews.

So when somebody shows you one screenshot where their company appears in ChatGPT and declares that they have cracked GEO, please relax.

One appearance is not a strategy.

The better approach is continuous experimentation. Identify the questions customers actually ask, measure how your company appears across those questions, study the sources influencing the answers, improve the information around your brand and repeat the process over time.

Measuring GEO requires more than traffic

Traffic still matters.

I would personally rather have 10,000 people visit a website and buy something than receive an imaginary trophy because ChatGPT mentioned the company 400 times.

But traffic cannot tell you everything when people can now research your category, compare your competitors and develop an opinion before clicking through to anybody’s website.

When I analyse AI visibility, I care about questions like:

  • How frequently does the brand appear across relevant prompts?

  • How often does the AI recommend it?

  • Which sources are being cited?

  • How visible are competitors?

  • Is the description of the company accurate?

  • Does the brand appear for high-intent questions or only informational ones?

  • Are visitors coming from AI tools eventually converting?

Tools and methodologies for measuring some of these things are still developing, so I would be suspicious of anyone pretending the industry has already settled on a perfect measurement framework.

The goal remains the same as most good marketing: understand whether the work is increasing the chances that the right people discover, trust and eventually choose you.

The easiest way I’ve found to understand the whole thing

When somebody uses traditional search, your website is competing to become one of the places they visit while looking for an answer.

AEO makes your information easier for search and answer systems to extract when responding to a quetion, while GEO expands the focus to how your brand, content and reputation appear inside AI-generated responses.

You have to think beyond a single webpage.

The machine may be learning about you from your website, somebody’s Reddit comment, a review platform, a journalist, your documentation, your original research or a combination of all of them.

Your job is to make sure the information surrounding your brand is clear, useful, credible and available in the places these systems look.

There is still a lot we do not know about how AI search will evolve, and anyone claiming otherwise is probably selling something.

I’m continuing to test how brands appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI and Perplexity, and I’m co-authoring the State of AI Search in Nigeria to understand what this shift looks like in our own market. You can sign up here to get the report when it drops, and I’ll keep sharing what I learn as this entire industry inevitably changes again next week.

item.title: OPay, Kuda and Moniepoint: What AI Recommends as the Best Digital Bank in Nigeria
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
When Felix Akinnibi and I tested how AI platforms understand Nigeria’s fintech market, one prompt felt obvious:

“Which digital bank is best for everyday use in Nigeria?”

We ran it twice across ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI and Perplexity.

“Best” leaves plenty of room for interpretation. Someone might care about transfer reliability. Someone else wants cheap transactions, a good card, POS access, savings features or an app that will not disgrace them while a cashier is staring.

The answers changed across platforms and between runs, although the way each brand was characterised stayed surprisingly consistent.

We use “digital bank” loosely here because the companies do not all operate under the same licence. The CBN lists OPay and PalmPay as Mobile Money Operators, while Kuda and Moniepoint operate as microfinance banks. Consumers still use them for many of the same things, so they regularly end up competing in the same recommendation query.

Run 1: What ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI and Perplexity Said

ChatGPT picked Kuda for everyday personal banking, while recommending OPay for people who frequently needed cash or POS access. Moniepoint was positioned around business and personal banking, while PalmPay got cashback and rewards.

The Kuda framing matched its product positioning. It offers 25 free interbank transfers each month, alongside cards, automated savings and spending tools.

OPay occupied a different space in the answer: convenience when everyday banking extends into agents, cash and physical payments.

Gemini skipped an overall winner and divided the category by use case.

OPay got everyday payments and transaction uptime. Kuda got personal banking and budgeting. PalmPay got cashback and rewards. Moniepoint got reliability and the crossover between personal and business banking.

The reader effectively had to choose which version of “best” applied to them.

That framing fits a market where the leading fintechs are already close on customer experience. In KPMG’s 2025 survey, OPay scored 80.7, Kuda 79.1, and Moniepoint and PalmPay 79.0.

Meta AI picked OPay for daily transactions. PalmPay was its preferred backup, while Moniepoint was recommended for security and business use.

Its case for OPay centred on transfer reliability, bills and the company’s agent/POS footprint. Meta interpreted “everyday use” as the ability to move and spend money without much friction.

Perplexity went back to Kuda, calling it the “best all-round digital bank for everyday spending.”

It widened the comparison beyond the usual four, introducing ALAT by Wema as another relevant option. ALAT was recommended for keeping a larger emergency balance, while Moniepoint Personal appeared for automated savings.

Its visible sources also differed from Meta’s. Perplexity pulled from Kuda’s first-party information and regulatory sources such as the NDIC, giving the answer more of a traditional banking lens.

Run 2: The Rankings Changed, the Brand Associations Mostly Didn’t

Then we ran the same prompt again.

ChatGPT switched to OPay.

OPay became the overall recommendation for daily spending, transfers, cards, bills and cash access. Moniepoint came second for heavy transfers and POS payments. Kuda dropped to third for budgeting and the banking experience. PalmPay came fourth for rewards.

The ranking changed, while the brand associations stayed almost identical.

Kuda still meant budgeting and personal banking. Moniepoint still meant payment infrastructure and POS. PalmPay still meant rewards. OPay still meant daily transactions.

ChatGPT’s visible sources in this run were concentrated around company websites, product documentation, app stores and regulators. OPay’s Google Play listing, for example, shows more than 50 million downloads.

Perplexity kept Kuda in first place.

It again described Kuda as the “best all-round digital bank”, citing low fees, free monthly transfers, budgeting tools and virtual cards. OPay and PalmPay appeared as alternatives for people who prioritised transfers, bills and agent access.

PalmPay had been less prominent in Perplexity’s first run, so even the shortlist shifted between identical queries.

Perplexity’s visible sources leaned more heavily towards third-party reviews and comparison sites than ChatGPT’s. Kuda has enough product evidence to support the framing, including 25 free interbank transfers each month, savings features, cards and spending tools. The final label of “best all-round”, though, depends on which of those attributes the model decides to prioritise.

Gemini put OPay first, followed by Moniepoint, PalmPay and Kuda.

This was the first result where Kuda fell outside the top three.

The same brand patterns remained. OPay got spending and bills. Moniepoint got uptime and merchant transactions. PalmPay got rewards. Kuda got budgeting and saving.

Gemini also added a regulatory status column. It identified OPay and PalmPay as Mobile Money Operators and Moniepoint and Kuda as microfinance banks.

That information introduced another factor into what had mostly been a product comparison. The CBN’s licensing information confirms the distinction, and the deposit-insurance treatment also differs by institution type. The NDIC provides up to ₦5 million in pass-through coverage per eligible Mobile Money subscriber, compared with ₦2 million per depositor at a microfinance bank.

Meta AI also chose OPay, calling it the strongest option for “pure everyday reliability.”

OPay got the recommendation for transfers, agents and POS. Kuda came second for app design, budgeting tools and free transfers. Meta cited its smaller agent network and reports of transfer delays among the reasons OPay remained ahead.

Its sources looked different from the other platforms. Nigerian media, comparison sites and social posts appeared prominently, including conversations where people were directly comparing OPay, PalmPay and Moniepoint.

Ifekoya, an SEO specialist at PiggyVest, had previously described Meta AI to me as an underrated surface for Nigerian marketers. The sourcing in this test helps explain why it deserves attention: Meta was pulling evidence from places where Nigerians were already talking about these products.

Its answer also contained a factual error. Meta grouped the providers under the same type of CBN licence and implied that the same ₦5 million NDIC coverage applied to all of them. CBN licensing data shows that OPay and PalmPay are MMOs, while Kuda and Moniepoint operate as microfinance banks. The relevant NDIC coverage limits differ.

A confident AI recommendation can combine a reasonable conclusion with inaccurate supporting information.

What the two runs tell us

AI recommendations move

ChatGPT switched from Kuda to OPay between two runs of the same prompt. PalmPay moved in and out of prominent positions. Even where the same companies appeared, their order changed.

A single screenshot showing your company “ranking first on ChatGPT” tells you very little about whether that position will survive the next query.

Repeated appearances across runs and surfaces give a stronger signal.

OPay kept getting associated with everyday payments, transfers and reliability. Kuda stayed close to budgeting, saving and personal banking. Moniepoint remained tied to POS, merchants and payment infrastructure. PalmPay repeatedly appeared around rewards and cashback.

Those associations survived the ranking changes.

A small group of companies dominated the recommendation set

OPay, Kuda and Moniepoint appeared throughout the tests. PalmPay featured often, although less consistently. Other Nigerian digital-finance brands rarely entered the conversation.

The market itself is less separated than the AI answers suggest. KPMG scored OPay at 80.7, Kuda at 79.1, and Moniepoint and PalmPay at 79.0 in its 2025 fintech customer-experience ranking. Only 1.7 points separated OPay from Moniepoint and PalmPay.

AI compresses those small differences into recommendations such as OPay is best, Kuda is best or choose Moniepoint for X.

Brands that appear repeatedly gain an advantage before the ranking even starts because the model already considers them relevant to the query.

For everyone outside that group, getting into the consideration set comes first.

Each surface drew from a different mix of sources

ChatGPT pulled heavily from company websites, help centres, app stores and regulators. Perplexity leaned more towards reviews and comparison publishers. Gemini mixed comparison sites with sources such as YouTube. Meta surfaced Nigerian media and social conversations more prominently.

There is much more in the full report

This was one of five prompts Felix and I tested for the Nigerian fintech category when co-authoring the State of AI Search Nigeria Report.

The report looks at how Nigerians use AI, which Nigerian brands appear in AI answers, and what this means for marketers, founders, media teams, and digital operators.

item.title: The 5 Critical Leaks Killing Your Startup's Growth (And How to Fix Them)
item.dc:creator: jeremiah
item.content:encoded:
Imagine you’re driving a sleek new car. It looks great, sounds great, and should, in theory, get you where you're going. But every time you hit the gas, it jerks forward, sputters, or stalls completely.

So you do what most people would: top up the fuel, clean the filters, even repaint it to give it new energy. But no matter how polished it looks, something underneath isn’t working.

That’s how most go-to-market strategies feel in early-stage or post-PMF startups.

You have built a solid product, created content, and shipped new features. Still, conversions are slow, sales calls fail to advance, and marketing efforts deliver minimal impact. Everyone stays busy, but the overall growth is weak.

The real problem is never on the surface. It is the misalignment beneath the surface:

  1. Messaging works well in internal meetings but instantly flatlines with actual buyers.

  2. The sales process looks professional but consistently dies after the first demo.

  3. Teams work hard but operate in isolation, pulling your strategy in different directions.

Most founders and marketing leaders are simply too close to the engine to notice what is out of sync. This audit framework solves that by giving you clear, external visibility. The five areas below will help you identify the precise gaps, eliminate the friction, and finally unlock the consistent growth you need.

Homepage Audit: Win the 8-Second Test

Your company's homepage is the first sales conversation most potential customers will ever have with you. They do not start by reading your blog or booking a demo. They scan your homepage for about eight seconds, decide if the content is relevant, and then they leave.

When clarity is missing on your homepage, every other effort fails. Website visitors quickly leave. No one books a demo. Your sales team wastes the first ten minutes of every call explaining what you actually do, instead of focusing on closing deals.

I have seen this issue slow down otherwise promising startups. They tried to sound innovative, but used vague language that impressed no one. Phrases like "Empowering businesses to unlock next-gen solutions" sound like every other software homepage. This tells the visitor nothing about who you help or what improvement they can expect.

Real-Life Examples of Instant Clarity

Figma's early homepage is a prime example of clear messaging. They did not use jargon like "collaborative design platform with real-time capabilities." They stated: "Where teams design together." Then, they showed designers working in the same file simultaneously. They used no jargon and no feature lists.

The message immediately filters the audience: you either care about design collaboration or you don't.

Key Audit Questions

Ask these questions to assess your homepage's effectiveness:

  • Can a first-time visitor explain who this is for within five seconds of landing on the page?

  • Does your main headline communicate a clear outcome, or does it only list features?

  • Do your images and visuals reinforce the central message, or do they create noise and confusion?

  • Is there one obvious next step (Call-to-Action), or are multiple buttons fighting for the visitor's attention?

What a Strong Homepage Hero Looks Like

A strong hero section—the first thing a visitor sees—must complete four actions immediately:

  1. Names the audience. (Who is this for?)

  2. States the outcome. (What changes for them?)

  3. Removes the main friction. (What pain do they avoid?)

  4. Gives a reason to keep reading.

Targeted Example Structure:"For [who], who want [outcome], without [pain]."

Example: "For People Ops teams scaling globally, who want compliance peace of mind, without bloated admin tools."

That single line immediately tells the visitor if the product applies to them. If it applies, they scroll down. If it doesn't, they leave. Both outcomes are successful because clarity works better as a filter than confusion ever will.

Fix-It Tips to Maximize the First Impression

Focus on filtering, not pleasing everyone.

  • Rewrite Your Hero: Use the structure: For [who], who want [outcome], without [pain]. Test this revised pitch on someone outside your company. If they cannot quickly repeat what you do, the message is not clear enough.

  • Cut Filler Words: Eliminate vague words like "innovative," "cutting-edge," or "AI-powered." These words mean nothing unless you connect them to a specific benefit. Loom does not say "next-gen video messaging." They say: "Record quick videos to replace meetings." One is empty marketing speak; the other solves a distinct problem.

  • Run a Five-Second Test: Show your homepage to five people who have never seen it before. Immediately hide the page and ask them what the company does. If more than one person gets the answer wrong, your core message is broken.

  • Watch User Behavior: Use tools like Hotjar or Fullstory to watch real session replays. Look for where users show frustration (rage clicks), scroll aimlessly (dead scrolling), or immediately leave right after seeing the main headline.

Messaging Audit: Lock Down Your Single Narrative

When your cold emails, LinkedIn profile, and website all promise different things, you are training people to ignore your company.

This problem is common. Your product team may talk about "infrastructure." Sales might promise "speed to market." Marketing could promote "innovation." As a result, customers hear only noise, not a clear story. They cannot easily explain what your company does, so they fail to buy, refer, or remember you.

Real-Life Examples of Message Discipline

Slack’s success stemmed from its message discipline. They did not shift between calling themselves a "team communication platform" and a "workplace productivity tool." From the beginning, their message was simply: "Where work happens."

This clear, consistent message allowed them to grow mostly through word-of-mouth because users could easily and accurately explain what Slack was to others.

Notion also maintains a disciplined pitch. Whether you see their advertisement, land on their main website, or receive a cold email, the core message remains the same: "Your wiki, docs & projects. Together."

Compare this to startups that constantly use vague words like "next-gen," "AI-powered," and "seamless." When your core message changes every week, you cannot build brand recall.

Key Audit Questions

Use these questions to check the clarity and consistency of your company's voice:

  • Does your ideal customer see the same core promise on your website, in your emails, on LinkedIn, and in sales presentations?

  • Can your entire team describe your value in a single sentence, and would all their answers match?

  • Is your company's main tagline specific and focused on the customer's outcome, or is it just generic language?

What Consistent Messaging Looks Like

Messaging must be locked down and outcome-focused.

  • Kill vague slogans. Replace phrases like "Unlock the power of finance" with results your customer cares about. For example: "Cut month-end close time by 40%."

  • The message must be specific and easily repeatable. Your customer should be able to tell a colleague exactly what you do in five seconds.

Fix-It Tips to Align Your Narrative

  • Conduct a Value Audit: Run a small exercise across three different team members (e.g., one from sales, one from product, one from marketing). Ask each person to write down your company’s core value proposition without talking to the others. If the answers do not match, you have a clarity crisis.

  • Build a Positioning Document: Create one required, simple document that clearly locks in who you serve, what you solve, and why it matters. Make this document mandatory reading for every member of the sales, product, and content teams.

  • A/B Test Your Promise: Test different versions of your core message across paid ads, email subject lines, and landing page headlines. See which one makes people stop scrolling and which one causes them to leave.

Funnel Audit: Close Your Conversion Leaks

Most funnels are full of small holes — abandoned signups, dead demo links, unclear CTAs — that silently kill growth.

For instance, I once worked with a SaaS company that had a polished demo page but no way to book immediately. Prospects filled out a form and waited 3 to 5 days for a reply. By then, most had moved on or forgotten why they were interested.

We embedded a Calendly link and cut the form fields in half. Demo conversion jumped from 12% to 42% in three weeks. The product, but the less friction between interest and action improved conversion.

Dropbox learned this early. Their original homepage had users sign up, confirm email, download software, and install before seeing value. Too many steps meant too many drop-offs. They simplified the flow to get users into the product faster and growth followed.

Key Audit Questions

Ask these questions to find where customers drop off:

  • Can users move from landing page to action in under three clicks?

  • Do your forms ask only what's essential, or do they demand too much upfront?

  • Are handoffs between marketing and sales fast and personal?

  • Are you tracking micro-conversions like scroll depth, form field drop-offs, or CTA hovers?

What Great Activation Looks Like

Slack proved the value of speed. Their time from sign-up to seeing value was under two minutes. A user could create a workspace, invite teammates, and send the first message before friction could kill momentum.

That speed converted free trials into paid teams much faster than competitors who delayed activation behind long onboarding videos or complicated administration setup.

Fix-It Tips to Boost Sales

  • Watch User Sessions: Use tools like Hotjar or Fullstory to watch session replays. Look for where users hesitate, click back, or abandon forms halfway through. These are your most immediate leaks.

  • Track Events, Not Just Visits: Set up event tracking in Google Analytics (GA) or Amplitude. Measure the difference between people who "landed on the demo page" and people who "clicked book demo." This shows the exact drop-off point.

  • Cut Form Fields: Reduce your form questions in half. Ask only for the name and email. You can gather more qualifying information later through conversation.

  • Embed Live Scheduling: Place booking links directly on the call-to-action buttons. Do not make people wait for an email reply. If they are ready now, let them book now.

Content Audit: Answer the Buyer’s Real Questions

Many startups confuse posting often with having a real strategy. They publish weekly updates and blogs, hoping for results. However, content that ignores your buyers' actual problems will remain unread and useless.

Your content must drive traffic, build trust, or move people closer to buying. If it doesn't, cut it.

I saw this problem early on at RemotePass. Our first posts were about us: feature descriptions, company news, and our own opinions. We thought we were clearly explaining our product, but we got no traction.

We changed our focus by asking "What is our customer desperately searching for late at night before a major hiring decision?" This led us to write content that addressed critical, real-world pain points like hiring in the UAE, how to choose a payroll solution, etc.

The result? Our search traffic jumped 159% year-over-year, and inbound sales leads doubled.

Key Audit Questions

Ask these questions to ensure your content addresses customer needs:

  • What are your Ideal Customers actively searching for or asking about right now?

  • Do your article headlines focus on your product features or on solving the customer's problem?

  • Do you use real-world scenarios and specific data to illustrate your points?

  • Does your content cite external experts, customers, or third-party data to build credibility?

What Highly Relevant Content Looks Like

Great content anticipates a buyer's question and answers it completely, building a path toward a decision.

Ahrefs is a prime example. They publish deep, technical guides on search engine optimization (SEO), comparison guides for tools in their category, and full playbooks on running content marketing campaigns. Every single piece connects to a specific buyer question or decision moment.

Their articles often include quotes from industry practitioners and data drawn from real-world SEO experiments, not just Ahrefs employees. This external perspective makes readers trust the advice much more.

On top of that, if a prospect searches for "how to do keyword research," Ahrefs has several related pieces that all link together, guiding the reader toward a free tool or a software trial.

Fix-It Tips for Higher Conversions

Stop guessing what your audience wants; start writing about the questions they are already asking:

  • Use Search Tools: Use tools like SparkToro or AnswerThePublic to find the exact questions your ICP searches for online. Write content that directly answers those questions.

  • Add External Credibility: Quote your customers, industry analysts, and non-paid practitioners. These third-party voices add authority that self-promotion cannot provide.

  • Show, Don't Tell: Do not simply say, "Improve your sales process." Instead, show concrete steps: describe what a broken sales process looks like, walk through the fix with specific actions, and include screenshots or actual data examples.

  • Build Content Clusters: If someone searches for a topic like "compliance for remote hiring," ensure they find 5 to 10 interconnected pieces on your site that answer related questions and link to each other.

  • Write Strong CTAs: Use specific, low-friction calls-to-action (CTAs). "Download the checklist" works better than "Learn more." Tell the reader exactly what they will receive and why it matters.

Alignment Audit: Unite Your Revenue Teams

Growth stops when your teams—marketing, sales, and product—do not agree on your goals.

Success depends less on new tools and more on stronger teamwork. When departments work separately, they slow down progress. Sales teams receive unqualified leads. Product developers build features customers never requested. Marketing runs campaigns no one supports.

I observed a startup where the product team focused on "data access," the sales team talked about "HR automation," and the marketing team promoted "global mobility." This disagreement resulted in confusing messages, confused customers, and a messy sales process.


Real-Life Example of Alignment

HubSpot achieved major growth by aligning its teams around the same customer journey.

  • Marketing focused on creating helpful content that answered specific customer questions.

  • Sales adopted an "inbound" methodology, acting as advisors who helped leads rather than pressured them.

  • Product built tools (like their CRM) that directly supported the free education and advice given by marketing and sales.

This consistency—every team working toward helping the same customer solve the same problem—turned their three departments into one smooth growth machine.

Key Audit Questions

Use these questions to check for consistency across your departments:

  • Do all team members agree on the Ideal Customer Profile (ICP), including the company type and customer mindset?

  • Do marketing, sales, and product regularly share customer feedback with each other?

  • Do all teams use the same core positioning language in their presentations, calls, and content?

  • Do the sales and product launch plans match, or does one team constantly react to the other?

What Good Alignment Looks Like

Effective teams share information and work from the same playbook:

  • A single, shared document (like in Notion) defines the ICP and is updated every three months.

  • Teams hold monthly calls or use shared online updates for alignment.

  • Sales call insights directly influence the topics marketing creates content about.

  • Sales and marketing strategy guides which features the product team builds first.

Fix-It Tips to Create Consistency

Align your teams on the customer experience and the language you use:

  • Host a Joint Workshop: Gather all teams to clearly map the customer's problems, the key phrases they use, and their main sales objections.


  • Use Sales Call Data: Record and analyze sales calls using tools like Gong or Grain. Use the exact words and phrases customers use to describe their pain in all marketing and product messages.

  • Create a Shared Calendar: Develop one calendar for all product and marketing launches and review it weekly. This prevents one team from being surprised by the other's actions.

The best businesses operate as a single unit focused on the customer. When teams agree on who they serve and why, they drive growth faster.

Ready for a Second Opinion?

I have run dozens of strategy sessions with founders and marketing leaders, helping them spot these crucial Go-To-Market blind spots in under fifteen minutes.

I can help you pinpoint the single biggest leak in your funnel or the point of most damaging message confusion.
